precepts.text: God looked upon the children of Israel and had respect unto them.
precepts.point: He that remaineth shall be for our God, a governor in Judah, and Ekron as a Jebusite: as David smote the Jebusites and Solomon levied a tribute of bondservice on those left in the land, they will be our servants. No oppressor shall pass through them any more, for now have I seen with mine eyes, as God looked upon the children of Israel and had respect unto them.

note.label: Zionism in the Face of Syria & Hezbollah

precepts.why:
Zechariah 9:8: “And I will encamp about mine house because of the army, because of him that passeth by, and because of him that returneth: and no oppressor shall pass through them any more: for now have I seen with mine eyes.” No oppressor shall oppress us any more; they will not pass through.

And “now have I seen with mine eyes” is the same as Exodus 2:25: “And God looked upon the children of Israel, and God had respect unto them.” In Egypt God looked upon Israel under their oppressors and had respect unto them, and then he brought them out.

So when he says now have I seen with mine eyes, he is looking upon us to have respect unto us. The Lord encamps about his house, the oppressor is stopped, and right after it Zechariah says “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion”, because the King comes.

precepts.text: A new king arose over Egypt and set taskmasters to afflict Israel with burdens.
precepts.point: Pharaoh's daughter knew the baby was a Hebrew's child by his circumcision, not his colour. Reuel's daughters called Moses an Egyptian.

note.label: False New Year: Doctrine Slayer - True Past Curses & Trauma

precepts.why:
“Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph”. This new king set taskmasters over Israel to afflict them with burdens, and then went further: “And Pharaoh charged all his people, saying, Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive”.

That is gator bait. They sacrificed our baby boys in the river to Sobek, the gator god. The white man did the exact same thing to us in the Florida Everglades: put our babies in a net, wait for the alligator to bite, pull the gator out and make shoes and bags out of him. Egypt did it to us first. They killed the males and kept the women alive, because the women do not produce the nation; the man does.

That decree is why Moses was hidden three months and laid in an ark of bulrushes by the river's brink, and why everything that follows was done in secret. When Pharaoh's daughter came down to the river in Exodus 2:5 and found the ark, she found one of the very sons her father had ordered cast into the river.

precepts.text: Moses married an Ethiopian woman.
precepts.point: Pharaoh's daughter knew the baby was a Hebrew's child by his circumcision, not his colour. Reuel's daughters called Moses an Egyptian.

note.label: False New Year: Doctrine Slayer - True Past Curses & Trauma

precepts.why:
When Pharaoh's daughter opened the ark, “she had compassion on him, and said, This is one of the Hebrews’ children”. How did she know? He was circumcised. You never read about Moses getting circumcised; he was already cut, because some of our forefathers retained that custom from our fathers. Outside of that, she would not have known the difference, because Egyptians and Hebrews were both black.

Then Moses fled to Midian and helped the seven daughters of the priest of Midian at the well, and they told their father Reuel, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds”. What did they call Moses? An Egyptian. The same way Joseph's brothers took Joseph for an Egyptian. Reuel, Jethro, gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.

Numbers 12:1 shows what that family was: “And Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married: for he had married an Ethiopian woman”. She was Ethiopian, so Moses' father-in-law was an Ethiopian, a priest of Midian but not a Midianite. Ethiopians are children of Ham, Kushites, the family of the Egyptians. A Hamite would know a Hamite when he saw one, and they still took Moses for an Egyptian. If he had been a white man, they would have known he was no Egyptian.

Paul passed for one too: “Art not thou that Egyptian”, the chief captain asked, and Paul answered, “I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus”. Moses passed for an Egyptian, Joseph passed for an Egyptian, Paul passed for an Egyptian. These are black people. That's the point.

precepts.text: Amram took him Jochebed to wife, and she bare him Aaron and Moses; the scripture names the parents of Moses.
precepts.point: A man of the house of Levi took to wife a daughter of Levi. These are Amram and Jochebed, the father and mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
precepts.why:
Exodus 2 says only that “there went a man of the house of Levi, and took to wife a daughter of Levi.” Exodus 6 gives their names: “And Amram took him Jochebed his father’s sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years.”

The man of the house of Levi is Amram, and the daughter of Levi is Jochebed. They are the father and mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

precepts.text: In which time Moses was born, and was exceeding fair, and nourished up in his father's house three months.
precepts.point: The woman conceived and bare a son, and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months. Goodly means the child was exceeding fair; there was something special about this child from his birth.
precepts.why:
The woman “saw him that he was a goodly child”. Stephen tells what goodly means: “In which time Moses was born, and was exceeding fair, and nourished up in his father’s house three months”.

Goodly is exceeding fair. And the three months Exodus gives, “she hid him three months”, are the three months he was nourished up in his father’s house. There was something special about this child from his birth.

precepts.text: By faith his parents hid him, because they saw he was a proper child, and they were not afraid of the king's commandment.
precepts.point: The woman conceived and bare a son, and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months. Goodly means the child was exceeding fair; there was something special about this child from his birth.
precepts.why:
“By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king’s commandment.”

Goodly, exceeding fair, a proper child: the same thing. His parents saw there was something special about this child from his birth, and it was by faith they hid him three months, not afraid of the king’s commandment.

precepts.text: The Lord doth put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel.
precepts.point: She knew the child was a Hebrew and no Egyptian because the Most High put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel; though both peoples were dark of skin, this was a child of the chosen nation.
precepts.why:
When the daughter of Pharaoh opened the ark and saw the child, she said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.” She knew the child was a Hebrew and no Egyptian. The Lord told Pharaoh why that could be: “that ye may know how that the Lord doth put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel.”

Both peoples were dark of skin, but the Most High put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel, and Pharaoh’s daughter saw it in this child.

precepts.text: Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined; she saw this was of the chosen vessel of the Lord.
precepts.point: She knew the child was a Hebrew and no Egyptian because the Most High put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel; though both peoples were dark of skin, this was a child of the chosen nation.
precepts.why:
“Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined.” The babe wept, and Pharaoh’s daughter had compassion on him and knew him for one of the Hebrews’ children.

What she saw was of the chosen vessel of the Lord: a child of the chosen nation, the people out of whom the perfection of beauty shines.

precepts.text: If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; the Most High sees the oppression.
precepts.point: He looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. He did not just marvel at the oppression; he used his position for his people, unlike many who hold a position of power today and will not risk it for their people. Moses is the ultimate revolutionary, as Christ is.
precepts.why:
“If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and violent perverting of judgment and justice in a province, marvel not at the matter: for he that is higher than the highest regardeth; and there be higher than they.” The Most High sees the oppression. Moses went out unto his brethren and looked on their burdens and saw an Egyptian smiting an Hebrew, one of his brethren, and he that is higher than the highest regarded it too.

Moses knew the Israelites were his brothers. He knew he was not of the Egyptian lineage, that there was something different about him. And he did not just marvel at the oppression: he looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. He used his position for his people, unlike many who hold a position of power today and will not risk it for their people.

Moses is the ultimate revolutionary, as Christ is.

precepts.text: By faith Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt, and forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king.
precepts.point: The same claim stands now: the remnant does not want the names of the captivity but the natural heritage of Israel, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of this land.
precepts.why:
Pharaoh sought to slay Moses, and Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh and dwelt in the land of Midian. Hebrews shows what Moses gave up in that flight: “By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter; Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season”.

Moses gave up his whole upbringing and position. In Egypt his head was shaved, his beard cut, his dress and customs Egyptian. He laid all of it down to be what he was called to be, an Israelite, “Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.”

“By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king: for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible.” Pharaoh sought to slay him, and he fled, but not in fear of the king.

The same claim stands now. The remnant does not want the names of the captivity but the natural heritage of Israel, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of this land.

precepts.text: The chief captain took Paul for that Egyptian which made an uproar; Paul answered, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus; the Israelites were mistaken for Egyptians.
precepts.point: Reuel the priest of Midian is the same man called Jethro, the father in law of Moses.
precepts.why:
The daughters told their father, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds”. They took Moses for an Egyptian by his dress, by how he carried himself, and by his skin: Moses was a very dark-skinned man, the same color as the Egyptians.

Israel was always being mistaken for Egyptians. When Paul was to be led into the castle, the chief captain asked him, “Canst thou speak Greek? Art not thou that Egyptian, which before these days madest an uproar, and leddest out into the wilderness four thousand men that were murderers?” Paul had to tell him, “I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city”. An Israelite, taken for an Egyptian, from Moses to Paul.

And Moses, who stood up against the shepherds and watered the flock, was a man of war, not a weak man.

precepts.text: Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him; an Israelite in Egyptian dress passed for an Egyptian.
precepts.point: Reuel the priest of Midian is the same man called Jethro, the father in law of Moses.
precepts.why:
Long before Moses, the same thing happened with Joseph: “And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly unto them”. His own brothers stood before him and “Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.”

An Israelite in Egyptian dress passed for an Egyptian, even before his own brothers. So when the daughters of the priest of Midian called Moses an Egyptian, it was nothing new: Israel looked like the Egyptians, and Israel was always being mistaken for them.

Reuel, the priest of Midian who called Moses in to eat bread, is the same man called Jethro, the father in law of Moses.

precepts.text: Thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them four hundred years; and afterward shall they come out with great substance.
precepts.point: Respect unto His chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons: the Most High renders to every man according to his deeds, tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil, of the Jew first and also of the Gentile, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom that was Hellenized; but glory, honour, and peace to every man that worketh good. The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion.
precepts.why:
God heard their groaning and “God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.” The bondage itself was part of what God told Abraham: “Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years”.

And the way out was told him too: “And also that nation, whom they shall serve, will I judge: and afterward shall they come out with great substance.” When Israel cried by reason of the bondage, God remembered that word.

That prophecy is about Egypt. It is not a date of release in this present day.

precepts.text: Ye shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the LORD your God, and none else: and my people shall never be ashamed.
precepts.point: Respect unto His chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons: the Most High renders to every man according to his deeds, tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil, of the Jew first and also of the Gentile, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom that was Hellenized; but glory, honour, and peace to every man that worketh good. The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion.
precepts.why:
“And God looked upon the children of Israel, and God had respect unto them.” The Most High has respect unto one nation, Israel: “And ye shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and none else: and my people shall never be ashamed.”

He is in the midst of Israel, He is the Lord their God and none else, and His people shall never be ashamed. That is the respect God had unto the children of Israel when their cry came up unto him, and Israel cries in this captivity today.

precepts.text: His grace and mercy is with his saints, and he hath respect unto his chosen.
precepts.point: Respect unto His chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons: the Most High renders to every man according to his deeds, tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil, of the Jew first and also of the Gentile, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom that was Hellenized; but glory, honour, and peace to every man that worketh good. The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion.
precepts.why:
“This the people saw, and understood it not, neither laid they up this in their minds, That his grace and mercy is with his saints, and that he hath respect unto his chosen.”

God had respect unto the children of Israel because he hath respect unto his chosen. His grace and mercy is with his saints. The people saw it and did not understand it, but it is written plainly here: the respect God shows is to his chosen.

precepts.text: Yet now hear, O Jacob my servant; and Israel, whom I have chosen.
precepts.point: Respect unto His chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons: the Most High renders to every man according to his deeds, tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil, of the Jew first and also of the Gentile, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom that was Hellenized; but glory, honour, and peace to every man that worketh good. The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion.
precepts.why:
Who are the chosen God has respect unto? “Yet now hear, O Jacob my servant; and Israel, whom I have chosen”.

Israel is the chosen. So when God looked upon the children of Israel and had respect unto them, he had respect unto his chosen, Jacob his servant, the nation chosen above the nations.

precepts.text: God will render to every man according to his deeds, to the Jew first and also to the Gentile: for there is no respect of persons with God.
precepts.point: Respect unto His chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons: the Most High renders to every man according to his deeds, tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil, of the Jew first and also of the Gentile, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom that was Hellenized; but glory, honour, and peace to every man that worketh good. The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion.
precepts.why:
Respect unto his chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons. God “will render to every man according to his deeds: To them who by patient continuance in well doing seek for glory and honour and immortality, eternal life: But unto them that are contentious, and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, indignation and wrath”.

“Tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that doeth evil, of the Jew first, and also of the Gentile”: the Jew is the southern kingdom, and the Gentile is the northern kingdom that was Hellenized. Both get tribulation and anguish for evil. “But glory, honour, and peace, to every man that worketh good, to the Jew first, and also to the Gentile: For there is no respect of persons with God.”

The nation is chosen above the nations, and God has respect unto that nation; but inside the nation every man is rendered to according to his deeds.

precepts.text: And so all Israel shall be saved: there shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob.
precepts.point: Respect unto His chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons: the Most High renders to every man according to his deeds, tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil, of the Jew first and also of the Gentile, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom that was Hellenized; but glory, honour, and peace to every man that worketh good. The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion.
precepts.why:
God heard their groaning, remembered his covenant, and had respect unto them, and the end of that respect is written: “And so all Israel shall be saved: as it is written, There shall come out of Sion the Deliverer, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob”.

The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion, who turns away ungodliness from Jacob. The cry that came up unto God by reason of the bondage is answered in him.

precepts.text: The daughters of Reuel said an Egyptian delivered us; Moses was taken for an Egyptian.
precepts.point: The difference was made plain in the plague itself: the houses whose firstborn died were shown not to be his people.

note.label: Exodus 11: The Death of the Firstborn Announced

precepts.why:
“that ye may know how that the Lord doth put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel.” A difference had to be shown, because Israel and the Egyptians looked alike. Nobody could tell them apart by looking.

Moses is the proof. When he delivered the daughters of Reuel at the well, they went home and said, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and also drew water enough for us, and watered the flock.” Moses, an Israelite, was taken for an Egyptian. Joseph was mistaken for an Egyptian by his own brothers the same way.

So the Lord put the difference in the plague itself: not a dog moved his tongue against Israel, and the houses whose firstborn died were shown not to be his people. The difference was never in the look; it was in whom the Lord spared.

precepts.text: The priest of Midian gave Moses Zipporah his daughter, and she bare Gershom; Reuel is Jethro, and the daughters took Moses for an Egyptian.
precepts.point: Jethro was not an Israelite; he and his kindred were not of the tribes.

note.label: Exodus 18: Jethro's Counsel and Righteous Leadership

precepts.why:
Jethro, “the priest of Midian, Moses’ father in law”, heard all that God had done for Moses and for Israel, and came to Moses in the wilderness with Zipporah and her two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. Exodus 2 shows who this man is. “Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters”, and when the shepherds drove them from the troughs, “Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock.” When the daughters came home their father is named: “And when they came to Reuel their father”. He sent for Moses to eat bread, “And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.” She bare him a son, “and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land.”

That is the same wife and the same son named here in Exodus 18: Zipporah, and Gershom, of whom Moses said “I have been an alien in a strange land”. So the priest of Midian who gave Moses Zipporah in Exodus 2 is the priest of Midian who comes to him at the mount of God in Exodus 18. Reuel and Jethro are one person.

Exodus 2 also holds one of the color scriptures. The daughters told their father, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds”. Moses was an Israelite, but he was taken for an Egyptian, because Israel looked like the Egyptians.

And Jethro was not an Israelite. He and his kindred were not of the tribes.

precepts.text: The priest of Midian had seven daughters who came to water their father's flock.
precepts.point: They did not speak against Moses when he was saving them out of Egypt, nor when he set Aaron over the men and Miriam over the women; the murmuring came from somewhere else and they took hold of it. They said, Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us? And the LORD heard it.

note.label: Numbers 12: Speaking Against the Man of God

precepts.why:
Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses “because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married.” Who is she? Go back to Midian. “Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters: and they came and drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock.”

This is where Moses came in the forty years he dwelt outside Egypt: to the priest of Midian and his daughters. The Ethiopian woman is one of these daughters, the wife the Lord allowed him to marry. A place being called Midian and the woman called an Ethiopian is no contradiction.

precepts.text: Moses was content to dwell with the man, and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter; this is the same woman called the Ethiopian.
precepts.point: They did not speak against Moses when he was saving them out of Egypt, nor when he set Aaron over the men and Miriam over the women; the murmuring came from somewhere else and they took hold of it. They said, Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us? And the LORD heard it.

note.label: Numbers 12: Speaking Against the Man of God

precepts.why:
“And Moses was content to dwell with the man: and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter.” The Ethiopian woman of Numbers 12 is still Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian, whom Moses married in the forty years he dwelt outside Egypt, and whom the Lord allowed him to marry.

Miriam and Aaron did not speak against Moses over her when he was saving them out of Egypt, nor when he set Aaron over the men and Miriam over the women. The murmuring came from somewhere else and they took hold of it: “Hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us? And the Lord heard it.”

precepts.text: The Most High looked upon the children of Israel and had respect unto them, so he does respect Israel by nation.
precepts.point: Peter opens his mouth and says the Most High is no respecter of persons, but in every nation he that feareth him and worketh righteousness is accepted, and the word was sent unto the children of Israel. "No respecter of persons" does not mean nations are equal, because the Most High plainly had respect unto Israel and chose Israel above all people; it means he does not respect persons in judgment concerning his law, so whether a man sins outside the law or inside it he is judged.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
Peter says, “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons.” That does not mean the nations are equal. “And God looked upon the children of Israel, and God had respect unto them.”

The Most High plainly had respect unto Israel and chose Israel above all people. He does respect Israel by nation. So “no respecter of persons” has to mean something else.

precepts.text: The Most High looked upon the children of Israel and had respect unto them, so he does respect his chosen nation.
precepts.point: Peter says "of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons," but that does not mean the Most High has no respect for his chosen nation. He is a respecter of persons concerning his chosen race, and what Peter means is that God shows no partiality in judgment, whether a man is poor or mighty.

note.label: Acts 11: The Gentiles Are Scattered Israel

precepts.why:
“And God looked upon the children of Israel, and God had respect unto them.”

The Most High does respect his chosen nation. So when Peter says “God is no respecter of persons”, he cannot mean that Israel is no different from the other nations. He means judgment.

points: A man of the house of Levi took to wife a daughter of Levi. These are Amram and Jochebed, the father and mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

The woman conceived and bare a son, and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months. Goodly means the child was exceeding fair; there was something special about this child from his birth.

When she could no longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, daubed it with slime and with pitch, and laid it in the flags by the river's brink. Bulrushes are the river reeds known as cattails.

His sister Miriam stood afar off, to wit what would be done to him. The movie tellings of this account do not give the full details; to get a full understanding of what happened in the days of Moses you have to read the scriptures.
The daughter of Pharaoh sent her maid to fetch the ark, and when she had opened it she saw the child, and the babe wept. She had compassion on him and said, This is one of the Hebrews' children.
She knew the child was a Hebrew and no Egyptian because the Most High put a difference between the Egyptians and Israel; though both peoples were dark of skin, this was a child of the chosen nation.
Miriam was crafty. She offered to call a nurse of the Hebrew women, and Pharaoh's daughter sent the maid, who called the child's own mother, and wages were paid her to nurse him.
The child grew, and he became the son of Pharaoh's daughter. She called his name Moses, which means drawn out, because she drew him out of the water.
So Moses grew up as an Egyptian, although he was a Hebrew.

When Moses was grown he went out unto his brethren the Israelites and looked on their burdens, and he spied an Egyptian smiting an Hebrew, one of his brethren. Moses knew the Israelites were his brothers; he knew he was not of the Egyptian lineage and that there was something different about him.

He looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. He did not just marvel at the oppression; he used his position for his people, unlike many who hold a position of power today and will not risk it for their people. Moses is the ultimate revolutionary, as Christ is.

The second day two men of the Hebrews strove together, and he that did the wrong answered, Who made thee a prince and a judge over us? intendest thou to kill me, as thou killedst the Egyptian? When a people is oppressed they take the oppression out on one another, and brothers become their own enemies; the same spirit answers correction among Israel today, pointing the finger at the one who corrects.
Moses feared, and said, Surely this thing is known.
When Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to slay Moses; but Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh and dwelt in the land of Midian.

Moses gave up his whole upbringing and position. By faith he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season. In Egypt his head was shaved, his beard cut, his dress and customs Egyptian; he laid all of it down to be what he was called to be, an Israelite.
The same claim stands now: the remnant does not want the names of the captivity but the natural heritage of Israel, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of this land.
The priest of Midian had seven daughters, and the shepherds drove them from the troughs; but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock. Moses was a man of war, not a weak man.
Reuel the priest of Midian is the same man called Jethro, the father in law of Moses.

The daughters told their father, An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds. They took Moses for an Egyptian by his dress, by how he carried himself, and by his skin: Moses was a very dark-skinned man, the same color as the Egyptians. Israel was always being mistaken for Egyptians.
Zipporah and her family were Midianites, not Israelites; Moses married a woman of the land where he dwelt those forty years.

Moses was content to dwell with the man, and he gave Moses Zipporah his daughter. She bare him a son, and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land; Gershom means stranger.
In process of time the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel sighed by reason of the bondage, and they cried, and their cry came up unto God, as Israel cries in this captivity today.

God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. The bondage itself was prophesied to Abraham: his seed would be a stranger in a land not theirs and be afflicted four hundred years, and afterward come out with great substance. That prophecy is about Egypt, not a date of release in this present day.
God had respect unto them. The Most High has respect unto one nation, Israel: He is in the midst of Israel, and His people shall never be ashamed.

Respect unto His chosen is not respect of persons. Within Israel there is no respect of persons: the Most High renders to every man according to his deeds, tribulation and anguish upon every soul that doeth evil, of the Jew first and also of the Gentile, the southern kingdom and the northern kingdom that was Hellenized; but glory, honour, and peace to every man that worketh good. The nation is chosen above the nations, and all Israel shall be saved through the Deliverer out of Sion.
